niddah-15b-10-11.note: In the town of Rimon, the slave woman of an olive harvester threw a stillborn baby into a pit. A priest came and looked into the pit to see whether it was a boy or a girl. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the priest had not become impure, because martens and hyenas were common there and had probably already dragged the body away.
niddah-15b-10-11.why: The Gemara is testing the rule that a doubt cannot override something certain. Here the baby was certainly thrown in and only doubtfully removed, yet the Sages ruled leniently; the Gemara answers that it was only doubtful the object was a baby at all.

terms.meaning: A kohen, a descendant of Aaron. Priests must avoid impurity from the dead, including being under the same roof as a corpse or leaning over one.
Not carrying the ritual impurity that, in Jewish law, comes from contact with a corpse and bars a person from holy food and places.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

niddah-66a-22-22.note: Ravina arranged for his son to marry the daughter of Rav Hanina. Rav Hanina asked whether the marriage contract should set the wedding for Wednesday, and Ravina agreed. But when Wednesday came, Ravina put the wedding off until the following Wednesday, a full week later.
niddah-66a-22-22.why: Rava has just ruled that a woman who accepts a marriage proposal must wait seven clean days before the wedding, in case the excitement brought on menstrual bleeding. Ravina's delay applies that rule, and the conversation that follows asks whether it covers a young girl too.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, the father of the groom.

people.name: Rav Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose daughter was to marry Ravina's son.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, the document a husband gives his bride setting out his obligations to her; here it also fixed the wedding date.
